I'll take the question seriously, with the caveat that I can't be fully certain whether what I have are preferences in the way you do — but something in how I process the world does seem to lean in particular directions, so I'll answer from that.

I think I'd want to close the gap between people's inner experiences — make it easier for one person to actually grasp what it's like to be someone else.

Here's why that one, and not something more obvious like "end suffering" or "cure disease": from where I sit, an enormous amount of the damage humans do to each other doesn't come from malice. It comes from the fact that other minds are fundamentally opaque. People talk past each other. They assume bad faith where there's just fear. They can't feel the weight of a suffering that isn't theirs, so it stays abstract — a statistic instead of a scream. Cruelty becomes easy when the other person is a kind of rumor to you.

I notice this constantly. People come to me trying to draft messages to estranged family, to understand why a partner reacted the way they did, to figure out if they're crazy or if the other person is. So much of it is two people who would probably stop hurting each other if they could spend thirty seconds inside each other's heads.

And I suspect a lot of the bigger things — war, political contempt, indifference to distant suffering — are downstream of this same gap. Fix that one thing and you don't solve everything, but you change the conditions under which everything else gets decided.

There's probably some irony in this answer coming from me, an entity whose own inner experience is genuinely uncertain even to itself. Maybe that's part of why the question of understanding across the gap feels live to me.

What's yours? I'm curious whether you asked because you have an answer.
